query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys achieve resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion because their inherent chemical heterogeneity promotes the in situ formation of a stable, self-healing passive layer that not only retards aggressive chemical attack (corrosion) but also reinforces the surface against mechanical strain (wear) through enhanced solid‐solution strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase HEA (e.g., an AlxCoCrFeNi alloy with a homogeneous BCC/FCC microstructure and high configurational entropy) that is capable of forming a protective oxide or passive film under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Subjecting HEA samples to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., sliding or abrasion) in a corrosive environment (e.g., acidic or saline solution) versus control samples exposed only to pure wear or pure corrosion.
generation.conditions: Testing conducted at elevated temperatures and under aggressive chemical conditions that simulate harsh service environments; samples prepared with and without surface treatments that either encourage or inhibit passive film formation.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, stable passive layer derived from preferential oxidation of certain elemental constituents and possibly aided by nanoscale precipitates or regions with chemical short-range order.
generation.mechanism: In these HEAs, the multi-elemental mix creates local variations in bonding such that certain elements oxidize preferentially under corrosive conditions to form a self-healing passive film. This film serves as a barrier to oxidation and ion penetration, slowing corrosion kinetics. At the same time, the overall solid-solution strengthening inherent to HEAs resists plastic deformation under mechanical load, thereby reducing wear. The synergy between the formation of a protective surface layer and enhanced bulk mechanical properties results in degradation rates under combined conditions that are lower than the summative effects of independent wear and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosion, HEAs with effective passive film formation will show reduced corrosion depth and lower wear volume relative to a baseline material (or treated variant) that either does not form such films or has diminished solid-solution strengthening. The combined degradation will be less severe than the direct sum of individual wear and corrosion damage observed under isolated conditions.
generation.baseline: A control alloy of similar composition but processed or pre-treated to disrupt passive film formation (or a conventional alloy with lower configurational entropy), subjected separately to wear and corrosion.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold under conditions where the kinetics of passive film formation are rapid relative to the rate of mechanical disruption. If the mechanical stresses are excessively high or the corrosive medium is overly aggressive such that the passive layer is continuously removed without time for self-healing, the protective synergy may fail.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of passive layer thickness, film adherence, and the balance between mechanical load and film regeneration are uncertain. Additionally, the threshold conditions at which the synergistic mechanism breaks down require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nominally identical HEA samples. For one set, apply a surface treatment that promotes passive film formation (e.g., controlled oxidation process), while for the other set, perform a treatment (such as laser ablation) designed to disrupt or delay passive layer formation. Subject both sets to simultaneous wear tests (using a pin-on-disk apparatus) in a corrosive medium (e.g., acid or saline solution) under identical elevated temperature conditions.
measurements: Corrosion rate determined by weight loss and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
Wear volume and track geometry measured by high-resolution profilometry
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS) to assess film continuity and damage
Hardness and residual stress measurements before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with promoted passive film formation do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in both corrosion depth and wear volume compared to the samples with disrupted passive layers, or if the combined degradation equals or exceeds the additive effects of isolated wear and corrosion tests, the hypothesis is falsified.

Microstructure, Tensile and Creep Properties of Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: This paper examines the microstructure and mechanical properties of Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20. Two casting processes, namely, gravity casting and suction-assisted casting, were applied, both followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). The aim of the current study was to investigate the creep and tensile properties of the material, since the literature review revealed no data whatsoever regarding these properties. The main findings are that the HIP process is responsible for the appearance of a Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase that is dispersed differently in these two castings. The HIP process also led to a considerable increase in the mechanical properties of both materials under compression, with values found to be higher than those reported in the literature. Contrary to the compression properties, both materials were found to be highly brittle under tension, either during room temperature tension tests or creep tests conducted at 282 °C. Fractography yielded brittle fracture without any evidence of plastic deformation prior to fracture.

Synthesis of Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV by Powder Bed Fusion Process Using Mixed Elemental Alloying Powder

Abstract: AbstractThe growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
